channel.title: Help: Questions Desk (new posts)
channel.description: Posts in the forum category "Help: Questions Desk" - If you've got questions about the sandbox, chat, formatting (wiki syntax/coding), or anything that involves the writing process and/or something you're currently writing, post here.

item.title: How to multi-class instances?: Re: How to multi-class instances?
item.content:encoded:
An article with a comparable issue is SCP-4812, which uses the placeholder class "See Below" and specifies in a memorandum.

Personally I don't think it matters all that much, unless your narrative is highly focused on the variance in containment difficulty or whatever. Just consider how much effort goes into containing all the anomalies in-aggregate and then chose the class.

It's up to you but there's no need to make things harder than they are.

item.title: How to multi-class instances?: How to multi-class instances?
item.content:encoded: I'm working on a draft with a lot of sub-anomalies. The main object is Thaumiel, but it has multiple associated anomalies that would be considered Euclid or even Keter if they were their own article. For pacing purposes it's important to introduce the Thaumiel object first, so it needs to go at the top of the page even though its not the hardest to contain. How should I go about formatting this? Can I list the class and ConProcs of the first item, run through the description, and then list another class, ConProc, and description for the sub-anomalies? I'm sure there have been other articles with this same dilemma but I haven't seen any.

item.title: How to add Audio to an SCP: Re: How to add Audio to an SCP
item.content:encoded:
You can view the Page Source of the article via the "+ Options" link at the bottom of the page, to see the code needed to insert the audio. You'd upload the audio file to the page the article is on, and use the wikidot code from the page you're using as an example.

That said, it's highly recommended that you get the concept reviewed before you start working on a full draft, so you can be relatively certain that what you have in mind will be well-received by the audience. If you immediately start recording/editing the audio and the audience isn't that interested in the concept, that means a lot more redos and legwork.

item.title: How to add Audio to an SCP: Re: How to add Audio to an SCP
item.content:encoded:
If you want to see how an article does something, scroll to the bottom, click "+ Options", and then click "Page Source".

You'll need to upload the audio to the page, same way you would an image.

item.title: Is it hard for everybody to get greenlights?: Re: Is it hard for everybody to get greenlights?
item.content:encoded:
Agreeing with the above, and noting that a lot of the time, especially for newer authors, the preference is to find a concept that they are really excited about and that they also feel they would be able to see through to completion.

Not every idea posted is something that would be easy or fun to write up, even for experienced authors. No one is forced to work on revising something if they don't want to, nor should authors push themselves to continue with a concept if inspiration and motivation have fizzled out. An important part of being a writer (especially as a hobby) is knowing when to shelve something for looking at later.

item.title: Writing help: Admin Post - Info - Open
item.content:encoded:
Moved to the Questions Desk forum, since this is a query about the writing process and not a draft for critique.

Please note that drafts are not greenlighted, concepts are. You should not be asking for greenlights on a full draft.

For tips on how to get a concept greenlighted, see this post:
http://scp-wiki.wikidot.com/forum/t-13282692/how-to-get-more-reviews#post-4623556

item.title: Is it hard for everybody to get greenlights?: Re: Is it hard for everybody to get greenlights?
item.content:encoded:
There's a few reasons for non-greenlit ideas outnumbering greenlit ideas, like people not doing followup or refusing feedback, but the main thing is that a lot of ideas just aren't going to work.

Creativity is a lot like rummaging through the discount bin at a game shop: there's a dozen "Hall of Duty"s to dig through for every clearance-price copy of that obscure game that you've been wanting to get for ages.

The greenlight system is in large part an attempt to help new writers dig through the bad ideas, while teaching them to recognize and refine the good ones.

Experienced writers do the same thing themselves, it's just that you get better at spotting and throwing out bad ideas earlier, and maybe figure out how to transmute bad ideas into good ones every now and then.

item.title: writing about a GOI: Re: writing about a GOI
item.content:encoded:
It's actually fairly rare for the first page related to a GOI to be their GOI format; usually they start in SCPs, get popular, and then someone makes the format.

Do whatever you want, though, there's no rule pertaining to it.

item.title: Why are all of my ideas too big: Re: Why are all of my ideas too big
item.content:encoded:
Best bit of advice I can give is to seek out inspiration from other big articles, to see how successful authors have executed their ideas, or to cut down some of the less important bits so it's more manageable (you can always re-add them later!). And it's alright to shelve an idea if you can't work on it now; I've found that for a lot of things, giving it time is the best thing, so you can come back fresh and with a new perspective.

If you've got big ideas, it means you're excited about the wiki's world, and that's always a good thing. Best of luck!
